facts.title: Cleaning Events
facts.text: Dust settling on solar panels slowly lowers their power. NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers got surprise 'cleaning events' when gusts of wind and dust devils blew their panels clean.

facts.title: The Power Budget
facts.text: Every spacecraft has a power budget. Engineers decide which systems get electricity first — life support always comes first, science and comfort come after.

facts.title: Ice Under the Soil
facts.text: In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander dug a trench near the Martian north pole and found bright white water ice just a few centimetres under the soil. Days later, some of it had vanished into the thin air!

facts.title: Making Oxygen
facts.text: On the ISS, a machine uses electricity to split water (H2O) into oxygen to breathe and hydrogen. This is called electrolysis — the same trade-off you make at Outpost 7.

facts.title: MOXIE Made Oxygen on Mars
facts.text: MOXIE, a toaster-sized experiment on NASA's Perseverance rover, turned carbon dioxide from the Martian air into oxygen. It made about 122 grams of oxygen from 2021 to 2023 — enough for a small dog to breathe for about 10 hours.

facts.title: Blocking Radiation
facts.text: Materials full of hydrogen, like water and plastics, are great at blocking space radiation. A few metres of Martian regolith (soil) also makes a strong shield.

facts.title: Radiation on Mars
facts.text: The RAD instrument on NASA's Curiosity rover measured about 0.64 millisieverts (mSv) of radiation per day on the surface of Mars. On Earth, people get about 3 mSv in a whole year from nature.

facts.title: Radiation on the Way to Mars
facts.text: During its trip to Mars, Curiosity's RAD measured about 1.8 mSv per day — the trip through deep space has even more radiation than the Martian surface.

facts.title: Radiation on the ISS
facts.text: Astronauts on the International Space Station get about as much radiation in one day as a person on Earth gets in one or two months. Earth's magnetic field still protects them a lot!

facts.title: No Magnetic Shield
facts.text: Earth has a global magnetic field that acts like a force field against solar particles. Mars lost its global field billions of years ago, and NASA's MAVEN orbiter found the solar wind stripped away much of its air.

facts.title: What is DONKI?
facts.text: DONKI stands for Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information. It is NASA's space-weather log, run by the Community Coordinated Modeling Center at NASA Goddard, and it tracks solar flares, CMEs and solar energetic particles.

facts.title: Flare Classes
facts.text: Solar flares are graded A, B, C, M and X. Each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before — so an X-class flare is 10 times stronger than an M-class flare!

facts.title: Fast Particles
facts.text: A coronal mass ejection (CME) usually takes 1 to 3 days to cross to Earth, but the fastest solar energetic particles (SEPs) can arrive in less than an hour. That's why early warnings matter.

facts.title: The Sun's Cycle
facts.text: The Sun goes through an 11-year cycle of activity. Near 'solar maximum' there are more sunspots, flares and CMEs — the Sun reached a solar maximum in 2024.

facts.title: Green Aurora on Mars
facts.text: After a solar storm in 2024, NASA's Perseverance rover photographed a faint green aurora in the Martian night sky — the first aurora ever seen in visible light from another planet's surface.

facts.title: Talking to Mars Takes Time
facts.text: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, but depending on where Earth and Mars are in their orbits, a message takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to cross between them. No live video calls!

facts.title: The Deep Space Network
facts.text: NASA talks to faraway spacecraft with the Deep Space Network: giant dish antennas in California, Spain and Australia. They are spread around the globe so one can always see the spacecraft.

facts.title: Mars Gravity
facts.text: Gravity on Mars is only about 38% of Earth's. If you can jump 1 metre on Earth, you could jump about 2.6 metres on Mars!

facts.title: A Day on Mars
facts.text: A day on Mars is called a Sol. It lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds — just a little longer than an Earth day.

facts.title: Thin Martian Air
facts.text: The air on Mars is about 95% carbon dioxide and is less than 1% as thick as Earth's air. That's why astronauts always need a pressurized spacesuit outside.

facts.title: Brrr!
facts.text: Mars averages about −60 °C. Near the equator on a summer afternoon it can reach about 20 °C, but at night it plunges far below freezing.

facts.title: Why Mars is Red
facts.text: Mars is red because its rocks and dust contain lots of iron oxide — basically rust!

facts.title: Blue Sunsets
facts.text: Daytime skies on Mars look butterscotch-colored, but sunsets glow BLUE. Fine Martian dust lets blue light pass near the Sun's direction.

facts.title: Olympus Mons
facts.text: Mars has the biggest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons, about 22 km tall — roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.

facts.title: Two Tiny Moons
facts.text: Mars has two small, potato-shaped moons named Phobos and Deimos. Phobos is slowly spiralling closer to Mars — about 1.8 metres every 100 years.

facts.title: The Big Storm
facts.text: In 2018 a dust storm grew to cover the whole planet. It blocked the sunlight that NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover needed, ending a mission planned for 90 Sols that lasted almost 15 years.

facts.title: Dust Devils
facts.text: Dust devils on Mars can be much taller than skyscrapers. Orbiters have photographed their twisting tracks criss-crossing the ground.

facts.title: InSight's Last Selfie
facts.text: NASA's InSight lander studied 'marsquakes' for four years. It retired in 2022 when dust covered its solar panels so much that it couldn't make enough power.

facts.title: Weaker Sunshine
facts.text: Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth, so a solar panel there gets only about 43% as much sunlight.

facts.title: Kilopower
facts.text: In 2018 NASA tested Kilopower, a small fission reactor. Reactors like it could power a Mars base day and night — even during a global dust storm.

facts.title: Nuclear Batteries
facts.text: Curiosity and Perseverance don't use solar panels. They carry a nuclear battery (MMRTG) that turns heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.

facts.title: First Flight on Mars
facts.text: On April 19, 2021, NASA's Ingenuity helicopter made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It was planned for 5 flights and ended up flying 72!

facts.title: 98% Recycled
facts.text: In 2023 the ISS life-support system reached about 98% water recovery — it recycles crew sweat, breath moisture and even urine back into clean drinking water.

facts.title: Oxygen Candles
facts.text: As a backup, the ISS carries 'oxygen candles' — canisters that release oxygen through a chemical reaction when lit.

facts.title: Space Salad
facts.text: On August 10, 2015, astronauts on the ISS ate lettuce grown in space for the first time, using NASA's Veggie plant growth system with red and blue LED lights.

facts.title: Open Science for Everyone
facts.text: NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) shares data from space biology experiments — plants, microbes, animals and astronauts — free for anyone in the world to study.

facts.title: Plants in Moon Dirt
facts.text: In 2022 NASA-funded scientists grew small plants called Arabidopsis in real lunar soil from Apollo. They sprouted, but grew slower and more stressed than plants in Earth soil.

facts.title: Which Way is Down?
facts.text: In microgravity, roots can't feel which way is down. Space biology experiments show plants use light and other clues to decide where to grow.

facts.title: Super Algae
facts.text: Spirulina is a tiny blue-green algae that grows fast, makes oxygen from light and carbon dioxide, and is full of protein. NASA studied it as a space food back in the 1980s.

facts.title: Salty Soil
facts.text: Phoenix discovered perchlorate salts in Martian soil. They're not good for people, so future farmers would need to wash the soil before growing plants in it.

facts.title: Snow on Mars!
facts.text: The Canadian Space Agency built the weather station on NASA's Phoenix lander. Its laser instrument saw snow falling from Martian clouds in 2008!

facts.title: Canada on Curiosity
facts.text: The Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) on NASA's Curiosity rover was provided by the Canadian Space Agency. It tells scientists which chemical elements are in a rock.

facts.title: Canadarm2
facts.text: Canadarm2 is a 17-metre robotic arm built by Canada for the International Space Station. It catches visiting cargo ships and moves astronauts during spacewalks.

facts.title: Canadian to the Moon
facts.text: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen is part of the Artemis II crew — the first crewed mission around the Moon since 1972 — making him the first Canadian to travel to the Moon.

facts.title: Practice Mars on Earth
facts.text: In NASA's CHAPEA project, volunteers lived for a whole year inside a 3D-printed pretend Mars habitat in Houston to practice growing food, fixing equipment and handling long delays.

facts.title: Your Personal Spaceship
facts.text: A spacesuit is like a tiny spaceship. It provides oxygen, removes carbon dioxide, keeps the right pressure and temperature, and protects from dust and tiny meteoroids.

facts.title: SAFER Jetpack
facts.text: Spacewalking astronauts wear a small jetpack called SAFER. If they ever float away from the station, they can use it to fly back.

facts.title: Grand Canyon x 10
facts.text: Valles Marineris is a canyon system on Mars about 4,000 km long — it would stretch across the whole United States!

facts.title: A Meteorite on Mars
facts.text: In 2005 the Opportunity rover found 'Heat Shield Rock', a basketball-sized iron meteorite — the first meteorite ever identified on another planet.

facts.title: Yellow Surprise
facts.text: In 2024 NASA's Curiosity rover drove over a rock, cracked it open and found bright yellow crystals of pure sulfur — something never seen on Mars before.

facts.title: Lava Tube Shelters
facts.text: Orbiters have spotted holes on Mars that may lead into underground lava tubes — tunnels left by ancient lava flows. Their thick rock roofs could one day shelter astronauts from radiation.

quiz.q: How strong is gravity on Mars compared to Earth?
quiz.explain: Mars gravity is about 38% of Earth's — everything feels much lighter there!

quiz.q: What do we call a day on Mars?
quiz.explain: A Sol lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds.
Iron oxide — rust — gives Mars its red color.

quiz.q: Which of these is a GREAT radiation shield?
quiz.explain: Water is full of hydrogen, which is excellent at blocking space radiation.

quiz.q: What does NASA's DONKI keep track of?
quiz.explain: DONKI is NASA's space-weather database: flares, CMEs and solar particles.

quiz.q: Which solar flare class is the strongest?
quiz.explain: X-class flares are the strongest — 10 times stronger than M-class.

quiz.q: Electrolysis splits water into which two gases?
How much power do solar panels make at night?
quiz.explain: No sunlight, no solar power! Batteries keep the base running at night.

quiz.q: How long can a radio message take to get from Mars to Earth?
quiz.explain: Between about 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are.

quiz.q: What are the names of Mars's two moons?
quiz.explain: Phobos and Deimos are small, lumpy moons.

quiz.q: Where is most of the water on Mars today?
quiz.explain: Mars's water is mostly frozen — in polar caps and underground ice.

quiz.q: What vegetable did ISS astronauts eat from their space garden in 2015?
quiz.explain: They grew red romaine lettuce in NASA's Veggie system.

quiz.q: Which country built Canadarm2 for the Space Station?
quiz.explain: The Canadian Space Agency provided Canadarm2!

quiz.q: What color are sunsets on Mars?
quiz.explain: Martian dust makes sunsets glow blue.

quiz.q: The air on Mars is mostly made of...
quiz.explain: About 95% carbon dioxide — not breathable for us.

quiz.q: What is the name of the giant volcano on Mars?
quiz.explain: Olympus Mons is the biggest volcano in the solar system.

samples.name: Hematite 'Blueberries'
samples.text: Little round balls of hematite found by Opportunity in 2004. They form in water — a clue that Mars was once wet!

samples.name: Gypsum Vein
samples.text: A bright white mineral vein. Opportunity found one called 'Homestake' in 2011 — water once flowed through cracks here.

samples.name: Olivine Sand
samples.text: Green volcanic crystals. Olivine breaks down in water, so finding lots of it means some places stayed dry for a very long time.

samples.name: Jarosite
samples.text: A yellow-brown mineral that forms in salty, acidic water. Opportunity found it at Meridiani Planum.

samples.name: Opaline Silica
samples.text: Spirit found nearly pure silica in 2007 — a sign of ancient hot springs or steam vents.

samples.name: Lake Mudstone
samples.text: Curiosity found mudstone in Gale Crater — layer after layer of mud from an ancient lake that could have supported tiny life.

samples.name: Clay Minerals
samples.text: Clays form when rock sits in water for a long time. They are a top target for finding signs of ancient life.

samples.name: Carbonate Rock
samples.text: Perseverance explores Jezero Crater, an old lake with a river delta, where carbonate minerals formed in water.

samples.name: Volcanic Basalt
samples.text: Dark rock from cooled lava. Most of the Martian surface is made of basalt from its ancient volcanoes.

samples.name: Sulfur Crystals
samples.text: In 2024 Curiosity cracked open a rock and found bright yellow crystals of pure sulfur — a first on Mars!

samples.name: Perchlorate Salt
samples.text: Salts discovered by Phoenix. They can help water stay liquid in the cold, but must be cleaned out of soil before farming.

samples.name: Polar Ice Core
samples.text: Layers of ice and dust at the poles record Mars's climate history, a bit like tree rings.
